newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US sees progress in checks on biological weapons.
newsitem.headline: US sees progress in checks on biological weapons.

text.p: A senior U.S. arms control official said on Friday progress had been made towards a verification protocol that aims to prevent rogue states or guerrillas from violating a treaty banning biological weapons.
The U.S. official, speaking to reporters after three weeks of negotiations, said President Bill Clinton's goal of reaching agreement on the protocol by the end of 1998 could be met.

But he conceded that major obstacles remained, including what he called moves by some countries to weaken the original 1972 Biological Weapons Convention, and attempts by others to link a new protocol to ending export controls now in place.

The senior U.S. official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, took part in the Geneva talks amid lingering Western concerns that Russia, Iraq and other states may still have stocks of banned biological weapons.
Hungarian diplomat Tibor Toth, who chairs the negotiating committee, has been charged with putting together a draft protocol for the next session in July.
Delegates from nearly 140 states which have signed the 1972 pact are trying to finally put teeth into the treaty, which bans a whole category of weapons of mass destruction.
"I can characterise it as saying some steady progress was made during this period of time," the U.S. official said, adding that no "major breakthroughs" had been made.

"The urgency with which some people view treating the Biological Weapons Convention and are trying to do all they can to strengthen it, indicates that they are recognising what we in the United States have recognised -- that there is indeed all too easy an access to this type of weaponry by both rogue states and potentially terrorist groups around the world.
"We need to try to do all we can to find new and better ways to forestall, complicate or otherwise diminish that threat."

Noting President Clinton had instructed the U.S. delegation, led by Ambassador Donald Mahley, to try to finish by the end of 1998, the U.S. official said: "That is the U.S. objective. Do I think it is a feasible objective? The answer is yes."
The European Union has suggested a mid-1998 target.
In the wrong hands, biological agents including anthrax, botulinum toxin and bubonic plague could be sprayed by aerosol to infect civilian populations.

But disease pathogens have legitimate medical purposes for use in vaccines and some therapies. This has left negotiators with the dilemma of how to protect biotechnology and its secrets under a verification regime.
"Very small amounts of pathogen can be a very potent biological weapon. Very large amounts of pathogen can in some instances be very necessary for therapeutic purposes," the U.S. official said.
He cited botulinum toxin, being researched for therapeutic use in treating muscle disorders, as a type of problematic pathogen with potential "dual-use" (civilian and military).
The U.S. official said there was a consensus among treaty states that confidential business information at non-military commercial laboratories must be protected under a protocol.

"Intellectual information in the biotechnology area is a much more fragile thing than it is even in the chemical weapons area. Many more firms are much smaller -- sort of boutique manufacturers that have only one or two pieces of intellectual property which are so valuable that they constitute the basis of the firm's existence," he said.
